50	
51	**Summary:** Completed Section 3 of the add-harnaas-foundation change — help groups, the explicit-attachment rule, the local --json flag helper and the stdout/stderr output contract — taking the change from 17/74 to 22/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.

54	- cmd/harnaas/cli/root.go declares the root's help groups (setup, then assets) in display order, and adds addCommand(parent, child, groupID) as the single way a command joins the tree: it declares the group on first use, sets the child's GroupID, and panics naming command and group on an unknown id — surfacing a wiring typo at construction instead of cobra's execute-time panic

58	- cmd/harnaas/cli/root_test.go covers section 3.5 and 3.2: the root declares no persistent flags and a subcommand inherits nothing; --json is accepted only on the command that declares it and fails as 'unknown flag: --json' on a sibling and on the root; groups are declared in display order and none is declared empty; addCommand rejects an unknown group; and an AST pass over non-test sources asserts the package declares no init, so the no-self-registration rule survives a gochecknoinits suppression

63	- Cobra renders a help header for every declared group whether or not it has members — verified with a scratch test showing a bare 'Empty Commands:' line. That is why helpGroups is a declaration list and addCommand declares a group only on first use: eager declaration would show empty headings for install and lint until their own changes land. The cost is that group display order equals command attachment order, which TestHelpGroupsAreDeclaredInDisplayOrder pins.
64	- Cobra's checkCommandGroups panics at execute time for a command whose GroupID names an undeclared group, but AddCommand itself does no checking — so a group declared after the commands that use it is a latent panic, not a compile error.
65	- Section 3.5's 'wrong positional-argument count prints the subcommand's usage' and 'an unrecognized subcommand exits non-zero' were already covered by iteration 2's main_test.go (TestReportErrorShowsTheDeepestSubcommandUsageForAnArgCountError and TestErrorSwitchClassifiesRealCobraErrors); only the persistent-flag and unknown---json assertions were still missing.

71	### Iteration 4
72	
73	**Summary:** Added the paths and logging foundation packages (tasks 4.2 and 4.3) and wired both into the entrypoint, taking the add-harnaas-foundation change from 22/74 to 24/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.
74	
75	**Changes:**
76	- cmd/harnaas/cli/paths resolves the project root by walking up for a .git marker — accepting the file form git writes in a worktree or submodule, and letting the nearest enclosing repository win as git itself does — through a pure Resolve(startDir) that takes a directory rather than reading one
77	- paths.WithDiscoveredRoot is the single sanctioned reader of the process working directory, carrying the resolved root or the failure in the context; the forbidigo suppression lives there, inside the abstraction the ban's message names
78	- paths.ProjectRoot(ctx) surfaces the discovery failure at the moment a command asks for a root, so --version, --help and an unknown-command diagnostic keep working outside a repository; a context that never established a root reports ErrRootNotEstablished as a wiring failure distinct from the user-facing *NoProjectRootError
79	- *NoProjectRootError is typed so a command can recognise the condition without matching message text, and renders as problem-then-fix: which directory was searched, then to run harnaas inside a repository or create one with git init
80	- cmd/harnaas/cli/logging writes structured slog records to a file under the user's cache directory (HARNAAS_LOG_FILE overrides it, HARNAAS_LOG_LEVEL sets the threshold, both documented at their only read site), never to a terminal stream
81	- logging discards records where the log file cannot be opened, rather than the reference CLI's fallback to stderr, and Open returns no error because there is nowhere to report one to — a warning on the terminal is the interleaving the log file exists to prevent
82	- logging.WithCommand and logging.WithComponent label every record with the command the user ran and the subsystem that produced it, ahead of the call site's own attributes; the API takes slog.Attr only, so every logged value arrives as a named field
83	- The package doc states the privacy rule as a hard rule with harnaas's own reason: the files it handles are a team's instructions and rules, exactly the content nobody expects to find copied into a log they did not know existed
84	- main.go establishes the project root and opens the log before executing the command tree, and records the run's outcome by exit code and error *type* — never the error message, because errors from later phases will quote the manifest that produced them
85	- Test coverage: resolution from a nested directory matching resolution from the root, the marker-file form, the nearest-repository rule, the outside-a-repository diagnostic naming directory and fix, context carrying and key isolation, plus logging tests that redirect stdout, stderr and slog's default logger and assert on cleanup that nothing reached any of them
86	- CLAUDE.md's logging section now records the two load-bearing decisions — discard rather than fall back to a stream, and keep the log outside the project — so a later change does not reintroduce either
87	
88	**Learnings:**
89	- Logging cannot live under the project: task 8.11 requires that after init no .harnaas/ directory exists and harnaas.json is the only file that appeared, so the log file must go under os.UserCacheDir. Task 9.5's 'redirect home, cache and config under t.TempDir' harness confirms per-user state is where harnaas keeps everything that is not the manifest.
90	- The reference CLI's logging falls back to stderr when the log file cannot be opened; copying that would corrupt a --json document, so harnaas discards instead. The uninitialised logger must also be a discarding logger rather than slog.Default(), which writes to stderr — a stray log call before Open would otherwise print.
91	- sloglint's attr-only: true is already configured in .golangci.yaml, which is the mechanical half of task 4.3's 'attribute-only API'; taking ...slog.Attr in the wrapper signatures makes it a compile-time guarantee at harnaas's own call sites too.
92	- staticcheck ST1005 rejects an errors.New string ending in punctuation or a newline, which rules out the problem-blank-line-fix diagnostic shape for a sentinel error. Giving the sentinel a small unexported type with an Error() method keeps errors.Is working and keeps the message shaped like every other diagnostic.
93	- sloglint also rejects slog.NewJSONHandler(io.Discard, ...) in favour of Go 1.24's slog.DiscardHandler, and gocritic's mapKey flags a table-test map key with leading or trailing whitespace — a case worth testing, so that table has to be a slice of structs.
94	- t.Chdir forbids t.Parallel, which is the practical argument for making root resolution a pure function over a directory: only the one test that exercises WithDiscoveredRoot has to move the process, and every other paths test runs in parallel.
95	- t.TempDir sits under a symlink on macOS (/var → /private/var), so a root discovered through the working directory comes back spelled differently from the path the test created; the paths tests resolve symlinks in their scratch-directory helper rather than teaching the package to rewrite paths.
96	- errcheck's check-blank: true makes `_ = f()` on an error a lint failure, so a deliberately-ignored error needs a real branch or a signature that returns no error at all — which pushed logging.Open to return only its closer, with the unexported open(path) keeping the failure visible to tests.
97	
98	### Iteration 5
99	
100	**Summary:** Added the palette and jsonutil foundation packages (tasks 4.4 and 4.6) and routed the --json output path through jsonutil's canonical encoder, taking the add-harnaas-foundation change from 24/74 to 26/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.
101	
102	**Changes:**
103	- cmd/harnaas/cli/palette is a zero-dependency package of base16 ANSI slot constants held as plain strings, so harnaas's colours are a request the terminal answers with the user's own theme rather than a hex value that is only correct on the machine it was picked on
104	- palette's semantic aliases (Accent, Accent2, Muted, Success, Error, Warning, Info) are what styles declare against, with the raw slot names reserved for colour that carries no meaning; the package documents that one Muted slot rather than a range of greys is what keeps de-emphasis reading as one level
105	- palette deliberately declares no body-text alias, and the package comment states why: body text stays unstyled so it renders in the terminal's default foreground and inverts with the background, where pinning White would erase every line on a light terminal
106	- palette's tests read the package's own source via AST so a colour added later is covered without anyone remembering to extend the test, assert every declared colour is a slot in 0..15, assert no alias name reads as body text, and assert no two semantic aliases collapse onto the same slot
107	- cmd/harnaas/cli/jsonutil.Marshal is harnaas's single JSON document format — two-space indent, HTML left unescaped so an ampersand in a source ref survives, and exactly one trailing newline — with the indent a constant rather than a parameter because the whole point is that a manifest and a --json document are not formatted differently for want of a shared default
108	- jsonutil.WriteFileAtomic stages the bytes in a sibling file in the destination directory, flushes them to disk, applies the permission and renames over the destination, so a reader sees either the whole old file or the whole new one; staging beside the destination is what keeps the rename a rename rather than a cross-filesystem copy
109	- WriteFileAtomic removes the staging file unconditionally via defer on both success and failure, and flushes the destination directory best-effort after the rename so a crash cannot leave new contents on disk behind a directory entry still pointing at the old file
110	- WriteFileAtomic delegates to an unexported writeFileAtomic taking the flush step as a parameter, giving the failure-path guarantee a test seam without a mutable global, so the injected-failure tests still run in parallel
111	- jsonutil tests cover the format line by line (indentation is what is under test), HTML characters left verbatim, the single trailing newline, a round trip, an unencodable value returning no partial document, file creation and full replacement of a longer previous file, permission application, an unusable destination directory, and the two injected-failure cases — previous file intact and nothing created — each asserting on the directory's entries so no staging file can survive under a name the test would have to guess
112	- printJSON in cmd/harnaas/cli/output.go now encodes through jsonutil.Marshal and writes the finished bytes, so the --json document and the manifest init will write share one definition of the format, and an unencodable value returns an error with stdout still empty instead of a half-streamed document ahead of the entrypoint's error message
113	- Tasks 4.4 and 4.6 checked off in openspec/changes/add-harnaas-foundation/tasks.md; 4.7 left unchecked because its accessible-mode and piped-stream clauses depend on 4.5's uiform and interactive packages
114	
115	**Learnings:**
116	- golangci-lint's std-error-handling exclusion preset already covers os.Remove and *.Close, so `_ = os.Remove(...)` and a deferred Close stay clean even with errcheck's check-blank: true — but Sync is not on that list, so the best-effort directory flush still needs an explicit nolint with a reason. This is the boundary that decides which dropped errors need a suppression and which do not.
117	- testifylint's encoded-compare rule rejects asserting an exact JSON string with assert.Equal and pushes toward assert.JSONEq, which would defeat a test whose whole subject is indentation and trailing newline. Splitting the document on newlines and comparing the resulting []string satisfies the linter and reads better, because a failure names the line that moved.
118	- Injecting a mid-write failure portably needs a seam: making the rename fail is platform-specific (POSIX rename over a regular file succeeds), so passing the flush step as a function parameter to an unexported implementation is the way to exercise the failure path on both Windows and POSIX. Unlike a package-level var it does not force the test to give up t.Parallel.
119	- On Windows the staging file must be closed before the deferred os.Remove can delete it, so the write/flush/close sequence has to close on every path including the ones where write or flush failed — otherwise the 'no staging file survives' guarantee holds on POSIX and silently fails on Windows.
120	- os.Chmod on Windows only toggles a read-only bit rather than storing the requested mode, so the permission assertion has to skip there; the file-contents and no-litter assertions still run on every platform.
121	- The `check` mise task fans out fmt, lint:go, lint:gofmt, lint:gomod, lint:mise and lint:shellcheck but not lint:licenses — that gate is a separate task, so a change adding dependencies has to run it explicitly.
122	
123	### Iteration 6
124	
125	**Summary:** Added the interactive and uiform foundation packages (tasks 4.5 and 4.7), completing Section 4 of the add-harnaas-foundation change and taking it from 26/74 to 28/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.
126	
127	**Changes:**
128	- cmd/harnaas/cli/interactive resolves whether harnaas may prompt from the command's own streams plus the environment — HARNAAS_TEST_TTY override, then go test, then coding-agent sentinels (CLAUDECODE, CURSOR_AGENT, GEMINI_CLI, COPILOT_CLI, PI_CODING_AGENT), then CI, then both streams being terminals — with the decision biased towards 'no' because a flag-driven path always exists while a prompt shown to something that cannot answer hangs rather than degrades
129	- interactive deliberately tests the attached streams rather than probing a controlling terminal, which keeps the question answerable on Windows and keeps it honest under redirection: `harnaas init > out.txt` has a terminal attached to the process and still must not prompt
130	- interactive.ShouldStyle is the single gate in front of the palette, honouring NO_COLOR and excluding TERM=cygwin, and is kept a separate question from CanPrompt because a run inside a coding agent must not be prompted and may still be styled
131	- Both decisions are split into pure cores (canPrompt, shouldStyle) taking getenv and the terminal answer as parameters, because `go test` can never present a real terminal and the exported functions would short-circuit before the environment gates were reached
132	- cmd/harnaas/cli/uiform is the only place harnaas builds a form, so accessible mode and the base16 theme are applied without anyone having to remember them; New takes explicit streams so prompts render on stderr and cannot corrupt a --json document on stdout
133	- uiform.Theme unsets the pinned foreground on titles and unselected options in both the focused and blurred variants so they inherit the terminal's default text colour, and points selection at palette.Accent — the theme declares no colour of its own
134	- uiform.Confirm returns ErrCancelled for a dismissed prompt rather than folding cancellation into a 'no', because the init spec requires a cancelled prompt to write nothing and exit non-zero while a decline is an ordinary answer
135	- uiform.Confirm consults the context directly before and after running the form, because huh reports a cancelled context as ErrTimeout and ignores the context entirely in accessible mode
136	- Test coverage: a table over every prompting gate including piped streams and the CI=false escape hatch, each agent sentinel individually, real os.Pipe and bytes.Buffer both answering 'not a terminal', the styling gates, accessible mode completing a prompt against non-terminal streams, cancellation reported separately from declining, and the theme's unstyled-titles and accent-selection guarantees
137	- charm.land/huh/v2, charm.land/lipgloss/v2 and golang.org/x/term added to go.mod, with the go-licenses gate confirming all 20 new transitive dependencies are on the allowlist
138	- CLAUDE.md's non-interactive completeness section now records the two load-bearing decisions — prompting resolved from streams rather than a controlling terminal, and a cancelled prompt distinct from a 'no' — so a later change does not reintroduce either
139	- Tasks 4.5 and 4.7 checked off in openspec/changes/add-harnaas-foundation/tasks.md, completing Section 4
140	
141	**Learnings:**
142	- huh v2 reports a cancelled context as huh.ErrTimeout, not ErrUserAborted or context.Canceled — its run() maps tea.ErrProgramKilled to ErrTimeout because a timeout is the only reason it cancels a context itself. Matching on huh's error alone silently misclassifies a signal-driven cancellation; consulting ctx.Err() is the only reliable test.
143	- huh's accessible path (runAccessible) ignores the context entirely and runs synchronously against the given reader/writer, so a cancellation arriving mid-question is invisible until the prompt returns. Any wrapper that must honour cancellation has to check the context after the run as well as before it.
144	- Accessible mode is what makes a prompt testable at all: the full-screen path needs a terminal to redraw, while runAccessible works against a strings.Reader and a bytes.Buffer. A test that sets ACCESSIBLE and completes a prompt on non-terminal streams is therefore a genuine assertion that accessible mode was honoured, not a proxy for one.
145	- huh's accessible PromptString breaks out of its re-prompt loop on EOF rather than looping forever, and an empty line falls through to the default — so a test can feed a bare reader without hanging.
146	- The reference CLI's /dev/tty probe plus raw-mode ioctl is POSIX-only and would need three build-tagged files that do nothing on Windows. Testing the command's own streams for terminal-ness covers the same cases portably and additionally catches redirection, which the /dev/tty probe misses.
147	- lint:gomod necessarily fails in any iteration that adds a dependency, because it runs `go mod tidy` and then asserts `git status --porcelain go.mod go.sum` is empty — uncommitted additions are indistinguishable from an untidy tree. The signal to check is that `go mod tidy` produced no *further* change beyond the intended one.
148	- golangci-lint accepted the whole huh/lipgloss surface without a single suppression beyond the two gosec G115 fd conversions, so the charm v2 stack imposes no lint debt on this configuration.
149	
150	### Iteration 7
151	
152	**Summary:** Added the data-only harness roster package (Section 5, tasks 5.1–5.4), taking the add-harnaas-foundation change from 28/74 to 32/74 tasks with fmt, lint and tests all clean.
153	
154	**Changes:**
155	- cmd/harnaas/cli/harness declares the Harness descriptor — canonical ID (a named string type so a source key or display name cannot be passed as a harness), display name, PerUserLocation, and ProjectEvidence — with claude-code as the only roster entry and Default pointing at it
156	- Project evidence is held as project-root-relative paths ('.claude', 'CLAUDE.md') rather than a predicate, so init does the stat calls and the roster holds no behaviour the install adapters could later disagree with
157	- Lookup helpers: IDs() and All() returning deep copies in the roster's sorted order, Lookup, Recognized, and HasPerUserLocation as the query manifest scope validation calls
158	- *UnknownError carries the id exactly as written plus the recognized list, and renders problem-then-fix so a caller can attribute the failure to an asset entry without matching message text; HasPerUserLocation returns that error for an unknown id rather than false, because a typo and an unsupported scope need different edits
159	- Tests cover the default being itself recognized, sorted and call-stable ordering, the unknown-id message naming the input and listing alternatives identically on every run, every entry being usable with relative non-escaping evidence, and callers being unable to mutate the roster through All() or IDs()
160	- Two AST guardrails over non-test sources: the package imports no filesystem, network or environment package (encoding 'data only, no write behaviour'), and declares no package init so the roster stays a readable literal
161	- CLAUDE.md records the two load-bearing decisions — the roster is data only with the caller doing I/O, and an unrecognized id is an error because the harnesses list states a guarantee rather than exclusivity
162	- Tasks 5.1 through 5.4 checked off in openspec/changes/add-harnaas-foundation/tasks.md

### Fetch archives over HTTPS, resolve refs over the Git protocol

Three ways to get files out of GitHub were available.

Per-file requests through the REST contents API are the obvious approach and the worst: a skill is a
directory, so each install needs a listing plus one request per file against a rate limit that is
punishing unauthenticated — a CI job installing a handful of skills would exhaust it.

Cloning handles private repositories and other forges naturally, but pulls whole history for a few
kilobytes of markdown and makes the cache a set of repositories to maintain.

Fetching the repository archive for a resolved commit is one request per repository and commit, has no
per-file budget, is trivially content-addressable by commit, and reuses archive handling the source
CLI already has. Refs are resolved separately over the Git protocol because that path has no API rate
limit and goes through the user's existing credential helpers, so a private repository works without
`harnaas` inventing an auth story. Resolve names with Git, move bytes over HTTPS.

[0004-available-updates-are-lint-errors.md](../../../docs/adr/0004-available-updates-are-lint-errors.md)
makes an available update a hard failure, which is only coherent if the lockfile retains both what was
*asked for* and what it *resolved to*. Recording the requested ref alongside the resolved commit is a
requirement of this change that exists entirely to serve that one.

### Containment is enforced by the kernel, not by string comparison

Both `.harnaas` reads and destination writes go through a handle anchored at the relevant root.
Validating a path and then opening it is a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race — a component can become
a symbolic link in between — and prefix comparison is notoriously easy to get wrong across platforms.
An anchored handle makes escape impossible at the point of use rather than merely improbable at the
point of validation, which lets the asset id, the source path and every archive entry name be treated
as one class of untrusted input.

### Digests cover paths as well as content

The whole-source digest is computed over the sorted set of relative paths and their content digests,
so renaming a file changes the digest even when no bytes change. Sorting makes the value independent
of archive order and filesystem iteration order. Per-file digests recorded alongside it are what let
`lint` say *which* file changed rather than only that something did. File modes are normalized rather
than hashed, because harness assets are documents and an executable bit carries no meaning worth
preserving — and preserving it would make the digest differ across platforms that report modes
differently.

Removing an asset from the manifest removes its installed files, so the manifest stays the single
description of what a project has, and emptying `assets` is a complete uninstall. Pruning is limited
to destinations recorded in the lockfile whose content still matches: if somebody edited an orphan,
deleting it would destroy work, so it is kept and reported. A shared destination another recorded
harness still claims is likewise kept — attribution is per harness, the file is one file.

### Requirement: Repository Archive Retrieval

Content for a `github` source SHALL be obtained by fetching the repository archive for the resolved
commit over HTTPS, rather than by requesting files individually, and SHALL be fetched at most once
per repository and commit per run. A retrieval failure SHALL name the asset, the repository and the
resolved commit, and MUST NOT be treated as the source resolving to empty content.

#### Scenario: Multiple assets from one repository share a fetch

- **WHEN** several assets reference different paths within the same repository at the same resolved
  commit
- **THEN** the archive is fetched once and every asset is extracted from it

#### Scenario: Fetch failure names the asset

- **WHEN** the archive cannot be retrieved
- **THEN** resolution fails identifying the asset, the repository and the resolved commit

#### Scenario: Network failure never yields empty content

- **WHEN** the remote host is unreachable
- **THEN** resolution fails naming the asset and the host, and no asset is treated as resolving to
  empty content

### Requirement: Transport Security

Every network fetch SHALL use HTTPS and MUST reject a plaintext or loopback destination, including
one reached by redirect. Redirects SHALL be followed only up to a bounded limit. Response bodies
SHALL be read under a size ceiling and MUST fail rather than truncate when the ceiling is exceeded.
Credentials MUST NOT be written to disk or included in any error message.

#### Scenario: Plaintext destination is refused

- **WHEN** a fetch would be made over a non-HTTPS scheme
- **THEN** the request is refused before it is sent and resolution fails reporting the insecure
  destination

#### Scenario: Redirect to an insecure destination is refused

- **WHEN** an HTTPS request redirects to a plaintext or loopback destination
- **THEN** the redirect is not followed and resolution fails

#### Scenario: Redirect chain is bounded

- **WHEN** a request exceeds the redirect limit
- **THEN** the fetch fails reporting too many redirects rather than following indefinitely

#### Scenario: Oversized response fails rather than truncates

- **WHEN** a response body exceeds the configured size ceiling
- **THEN** the fetch fails reporting the limit, and no partial content is used

#### Scenario: Credentials are redacted from errors

- **WHEN** a fetch fails against a URL that carried credentials
- **THEN** the reported error contains the destination with its credentials removed

### Requirement: Archive Extraction Safety

Extraction SHALL take only the subtree named by the source's path and SHALL reject any archive entry
whose destination would fall outside the extraction root, including entries using absolute paths or
upward traversal. Symbolic-link, hard-link and device entries MUST be rejected rather than
materialized. Individual entry sizes and the total extracted size SHALL be bounded.

#### Scenario: Only the declared subtree is extracted

- **WHEN** a source names a path within a repository
- **THEN** only files under that path are extracted, and the extracted paths are relative to it

#### Scenario: Traversing entry is rejected

- **WHEN** an archive contains an entry whose path escapes the extraction root
- **THEN** extraction fails reporting the offending entry and nothing is written outside the root

#### Scenario: Link entry is rejected

- **WHEN** an archive contains a symbolic-link or hard-link entry within the selected subtree

#### Scenario: Extraction size ceiling is enforced

- **WHEN** the selected subtree exceeds the total extraction size ceiling
- **THEN** extraction fails reporting the limit and no partially extracted content is used

#### Scenario: Missing path in repository is reported

- **WHEN** the source's path does not exist at the resolved commit
- **THEN** resolution fails naming the asset, the path and the commit

### Requirement: Local Source Reading

validation. A source that does not exist SHALL fail naming the expected path relative to the project

#### Scenario: Local file is read

- **WHEN** an asset declares a local source that exists under `.harnaas`
- **THEN** its content is read and made available for installation

168		return f.fetch(ctx, rawURL, maxResponseBytes)
169	}
170	
171	// fetch is [Fetcher.Fetch] with the ceiling as a parameter, so the failure past
172	// it can be exercised without serving 64 MiB.
173	func (f *Fetcher) fetch(ctx context.Context, rawURL string, limit int64) ([]byte, error) {
174		// Checked before the request is built, so a refused destination is a
175		// destination nothing was ever sent to.
176		if err := f.rule.check(rawURL); err != nil {
177			return nil, err
178		}
179	
180		req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, rawURL, nil)
181		if err != nil {
182			return nil, &FetchError{URL: rawURL, Err: err}
183		}
184	
185		resp, err := f.client.Do(req)
186		if err != nil {
187			return nil, refusalOrFetchError(rawURL, err)
188		}
189		defer resp.Body.Close()
190	
191		if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
192			return nil, &StatusError{URL: rawURL, StatusCode: resp.StatusCode, Status: resp.Status}
193		}
194	
195		body, err := readWithinLimit(resp.Body, limit)
196		switch {
197		case errors.Is(err, errBodyTooLarge):
198			return nil, &ResponseTooLargeError{URL: rawURL, Limit: limit}
199		case err != nil:
200			return nil, &FetchError{URL: rawURL, Err: err}
201		}
202		return body, nil
203	}
204	
205	// readWithinLimit reads r to its end, or fails reporting that it did not.
206	//
207	// One byte past the limit is read deliberately. A bare [io.LimitReader] stops at
208	// the limit and reports success, so an oversized body arrives truncated and
209	// indistinguishable from a complete one — which for an archive means a corrupt
210	// source whose digest is recorded as though it were the real content.
211	func readWithinLimit(r io.Reader, limit int64) ([]byte, error) {
212		body, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(r, limit+1))
213		if err != nil {
214			return nil, fmt.Errorf("read response body: %w", err)
215		}
216		if int64(len(body)) > limit {
217			return nil, errBodyTooLarge
218		}
219		return body, nil
220	}
221	
222	// refusalOrFetchError surfaces a refusal the redirect policy raised as itself.
223	//
224	// The client wraps whatever [http.Client.CheckRedirect] returned in a
225	// [url.Error], whose own message restates the URL — the unredacted one. Returning
226	// harnaas's error rather than the wrapper keeps the message the user reads the
227	// finished diagnostic the rule wrote, and keeps the credential out of it.
228	func refusalOrFetchError(rawURL string, err error) error {
229		var insecure *InsecureDestinationError
230		if errors.As(err, &insecure) {
231			return insecure
232		}
233	
234		var tooMany *TooManyRedirectsError
235		if errors.As(err, &tooMany) {
236			return tooMany
237		}
238	
239		return &FetchError{URL: rawURL, Err: err}
240	}

242	// InsecureDestinationError reports a fetch harnaas refused to make because of
243	// where it pointed, whether that was the URL it built or somewhere a redirect
244	// sent it.
245	type InsecureDestinationError struct {
246		// URL is the refused destination, held exactly as it was written and
247		// redacted where the message is built. Holding the raw value and redacting
248		// at the one place it renders is what makes redaction a property of the type
249		// rather than a step every caller constructing one has to remember.
250		URL string
251	
252		// Reason completes "refused ... because ...", naming which clause of the
253		// rule the destination failed.
254		Reason string
255	}
256	
257	// Error states the problem and then the fix, as every user-facing diagnostic
258	// does.
259	func (e *InsecureDestinationError) Error() string {
260		return fmt.Sprintf(
261			"refusing to fetch %s because %s\n\n"+
262				"harnaas fetches a source over https from a host other than this machine. "+
263				"Declare a source it can reach that way, or put the content in a directory under .harnaas and declare it as a local source.",
264			RedactURL(e.URL), e.Reason,
265		)
266	}
267	
268	// TooManyRedirectsError reports a chain that never arrived anywhere.
269	type TooManyRedirectsError struct {
270		// URL is where the chain started, held raw and redacted where it renders.
271		URL string
272	
273		// Limit is the number of redirects harnaas followed before stopping.
274		Limit int
275	}
276	
277	// Error states the problem and then the fix.
278	func (e *TooManyRedirectsError) Error() string {
279		return fmt.Sprintf(
280			"fetching %s followed %d redirects without arriving\n\n"+
281				"The host is redirecting in a loop or through more hops than harnaas follows. "+
282				"Check that the manifest names the repository directly rather than a URL that forwards to it.",
283			RedactURL(e.URL), e.Limit,
284		)
285	}
286	
287	// ResponseTooLargeError reports a body past the size ceiling.
288	type ResponseTooLargeError struct {
289		// URL is the destination that served it, held raw and redacted where it
290		// renders.
291		URL string
292	
293		// Limit is the ceiling in bytes, so the message states the number the
294		// response has to come under rather than only that it did not.
295		Limit int64
296	}
297	
298	// Error states the problem and then the fix.
299	func (e *ResponseTooLargeError) Error() string {
300		return fmt.Sprintf(
301			"%s served more than the %d bytes harnaas reads from one source\n\n"+
302				"Harness assets are documents, so a source this large is nearly always a repository that happens to contain them rather than the repository they live in. "+
303				"Declare a source that holds the assets themselves.",
304			RedactURL(e.URL), e.Limit,
305		)
306	}
307	
308	// StatusError reports a response harnaas will not read.
309	//
310	// It is deliberately a plain transport diagnostic: the kind that made the request
311	// is the only thing that knows which asset, repository and commit the URL stood
312	// for, so it is what turns a 404 into a message about a missing path.
313	type StatusError struct {
314		// URL is the destination, held raw and redacted where it renders.
315		URL string
316	
317		// StatusCode is the response status, kept as a number so a caller can
318		// recognize the cases it has something better to say about.
319		StatusCode int
320	
321		// Status is the status line, which carries the host's own wording.
322		Status string
323	}
324	
325	// Error states the problem and then the fix.
326	func (e *StatusError) Error() string {
327		return fmt.Sprintf(
328			"%s answered %s\n\n"+
329				"Check that the source the manifest declares exists and is readable, then run harnaas install again.",
330			RedactURL(e.URL), e.Status,
331		)
332	}
333	
334	// FetchError reports a request that produced no usable response at all.
335	type FetchError struct {
336		// URL is the destination, held raw and redacted where it renders.
337		URL string
338	
339		// Err is the underlying failure, kept so a caller can recognize a cancelled
340		// run through errors.Is.
341		Err error
342	}
343	
344	// Error states the problem and then the fix.
345	//
346	// The cause is unwrapped out of its [url.Error] first. That wrapper's own message
347	// restates the URL unredacted, so quoting it would put back exactly what
348	// [RedactURL] exists to remove — and it adds nothing, since the destination is
349	// already the first thing this message names.
350	func (e *FetchError) Error() string {
351		cause := e.Err
352	
353		var wrapped *url.Error
354		if errors.As(cause, &wrapped) {
355			cause = wrapped.Err
356		}
357	
358		return fmt.Sprintf(
359			"could not fetch %s: %s\n\n"+
360				"Check that this machine can reach the host, then run harnaas install again.",
361			RedactURL(e.URL), cause,
362		)
363	}
364	
365	// Unwrap keeps the cause reachable, so a fetch ended by an interrupt is still
366	// recognizable as a cancelled context rather than as a network failure.
367	func (e *FetchError) Unwrap() error { return e.Err }

11	// Scope is where an asset's installed copy lives: beside the project, or in the
12	// target harness's own per-user location.
13	//
14	// It is declared per asset rather than chosen per run because it is a property
15	// of the content — a team's house-style rule belongs to the repository, a
16	// personal shortcut belongs to the person — and a flag would make one manifest
17	// install to two different places depending on who ran the command.
18	type Scope string
19	
20	const (
21		// ScopeProject installs beneath the project root of each target harness. It
22		// is the default, and the only scope an instruction may take.
23		ScopeProject Scope = "project"
24	
25		// ScopeUser installs into the target harness's per-user location, and is
26		// accepted only for a harness the roster records as having an unambiguous
27		// one.
28		ScopeUser Scope = "user"
29	)

31	// scopes is every accepted scope, in the order every diagnostic lists them —
32	// the default first, because it is the one an author reading the list most
33	// often wants.
34	var scopes = []Scope{ScopeProject, ScopeUser}

36	// Asset is one manifest entry with every question about it answered: what it
37	// is, what it is called, which harnesses it is guaranteed for, and where it
38	// installs.
39	//
40	// Nothing here is optional. Every field an entry may leave undeclared has been
41	// inferred from its path or defaulted from the document by the time an Asset
42	// exists, which is what makes it the shape later phases read: `install` never
43	// has to know whether the author wrote `type` or relied on the directory name,
44	// and so cannot treat the two differently.
45	type Asset struct {
46		// Index is the entry's position in the `assets` array, carried through
47		// because it stays the way every diagnostic points at the line to edit.
48		Index int
49	
50		// ObjectForm records whether the entry was written as an object, so a
51		// remedy can direct an author to the object form only when they are not
52		// already using it.
53		ObjectForm bool
54	
55		// Ref is the parsed source string: which source, and the path within it.
56		Ref AssetRef
57	
58		// Type is the asset's type, declared or inferred from the containing
59		// directory.
60		Type AssetType
61	
62		// ID is the asset's id, declared or inferred from the path's leaf.
63		ID string
64	
65		// Targets is the effective target list: the entry's own `targets` where it
66		// declared them, and the manifest's `harnesses` otherwise. It is never
67		// empty — an asset with no target could never be installed anywhere, which
68		// is a violation rather than a state an Asset can reach.
69		Targets []harness.ID
70	
71		// Scope is where the asset installs, `project` unless the entry declared
72		// otherwise.
73		Scope Scope
74	}

76	// ResolveType returns the entry's type: the one it declares, or the one its
77	// path implies.
78	//
79	// A declared type suppresses inference entirely rather than being checked
80	// against it. The object form exists precisely for a source whose layout does
81	// not follow the convention, so comparing the two would refuse the case it was
82	// added for.
83	func ResolveType(entry AssetEntry, ref AssetRef) (AssetType, *Violation) {
84		if entry.Type == "" {
85			return InferType(entry.Index, ref)
86		}
87	
88		declared := AssetType(entry.Type)
89		if !slices.Contains(AssetTypes(), declared) {
90			return "", assetViolation(entry.Index, "type",
91				fmt.Sprintf("%s declares the type %q, which is not a type harnaas installs", assetSubject(entry.Index), entry.Type),
92				fmt.Sprintf("Set %q on the entry in %s to one of %s.", "type", FileName, typeList()),
93			)
94		}
95	
96		return declared, nil
97	}

99	// ResolveID returns the entry's id: the one it declares, or the one its path's
100	// leaf implies.
101	//
102	// Inference is suppressed one field at a time, which is why this is a separate
103	// decision from [ResolveType]: an entry declaring `type` for an unconventional
104	// layout still wants its id inferred, and an entry declaring `id` because two
105	// sources use the same leaf still wants its type inferred.
106	//
107	// Whether the resulting id is usable — a single safe path segment, unique among
108	// assets of its type — is a question about the document rather than the entry,
109	// and is answered where every entry's id is in hand.
110	func ResolveID(entry AssetEntry, ref AssetRef) (string, *Violation) {
111		if entry.ID == "" {
112			return InferID(entry.Index, ref)
113		}
114		return entry.ID, nil
115	}

117	// ResolveTargets returns the harnesses an entry is guaranteed for: its own
118	// `targets` where it declared them, and the manifest's `harnesses` otherwise.
119	//
120	// A name inherited from `harnesses` is not checked here. It is checked once by
121	// [CheckHarnesses], because a misspelling in that one list is one mistake, and
122	// attributing it to every asset that inherited it would report the same edit
123	// once per entry and bury the entries with problems of their own.
124	//
125	// The result is a list of violations rather than one because `targets` is
126	// itself a list: two unrecognized names are two independent edits, and each is
127	// attributed to its own position so the aggregate orders them the same way on
128	// every run.
129	func ResolveTargets(entry AssetEntry, harnesses []string) ([]harness.ID, []*Violation) {
130		// A nil slice is an undeclared field and an empty one is a declared empty
131		// list. Both leave the asset with nowhere to install, but the edit that
132		// fixes them is different, so decoding kept them distinguishable and this
133		// is where the distinction is spent.
134		if entry.Targets == nil {
135			if len(harnesses) == 0 {
136				return nil, []*Violation{assetViolation(entry.Index, "targets",
137					fmt.Sprintf(
138						"%s has no target harness: it declares no %q and the manifest declares no %q",
139						assetSubject(entry.Index), "targets", "harnesses",
140					),
141					fmt.Sprintf(
142						"Add a %q list to %s naming at least one of %s, or declare %q on this entry.",
143						"harnesses", FileName, harnessList(), "targets",
144					),
145				)}
146			}
147			return toHarnessIDs(harnesses), nil
148		}
149	
150		if len(entry.Targets) == 0 {
151			return nil, []*Violation{assetViolation(entry.Index, "targets",
152				fmt.Sprintf(
153					"%s declares an empty %q list, so it could never be installed anywhere",
154					assetSubject(entry.Index), "targets",
155				),
156				fmt.Sprintf(
157					"Name at least one of %s in the entry's %q, or remove the field so the asset inherits the manifest's %q.",
158					harnessList(), "targets", "harnesses",
159				),
160			)}
161		}
162	
163		var violations []*Violation
164		targets := make([]harness.ID, 0, len(entry.Targets))
165		for position, name := range entry.Targets {
166			id := harness.ID(name)
167			if !harness.Recognized(id) {
168				violations = append(violations, assetViolation(entry.Index, fmt.Sprintf("targets[%d]", position),
169					fmt.Sprintf(
170						"%s targets %q, which is not a harness harnaas recognizes",
171						assetSubject(entry.Index), name,
172					),
173					fmt.Sprintf("Change it in %s to a harness harnaas recognizes: %s.", FileName, harnessList()),
174				))
175				continue
176			}
177			targets = append(targets, id)
178		}
179		if len(violations) > 0 {
180			return nil, violations
181		}
182	
183		return targets, nil
184	}

186	// CheckHarnesses reports every name in the manifest's `harnesses` list the
187	// roster does not recognize.
188	//
189	// An empty list is not reported here. It is only a problem for an asset that
190	// would have inherited it, and an asset declaring its own `targets` is
191	// perfectly well served by a manifest that declares no default — so the
192	// violation belongs to the entry that has nowhere to go, not to the document.
193	func CheckHarnesses(harnesses []string) []*Violation {
194		var violations []*Violation
195		for position, name := range harnesses {
196			if harness.Recognized(harness.ID(name)) {
197				continue
198			}
199	
200			violations = append(violations, &Violation{
201				Index: DocumentIndex,
202				Field: fmt.Sprintf("harnesses[%d]", position),
203				Problem: fmt.Sprintf(
204					"the %q list names %q, which is not a harness harnaas recognizes",
205					"harnesses", name,
206				),
207				Fix: fmt.Sprintf("Change it in %s to a harness harnaas recognizes: %s.", FileName, harnessList()),
208			})
209		}
210		return violations
211	}

213	// ResolveScope returns where the entry installs: the scope it declares, or
214	// `project`.
215	func ResolveScope(entry AssetEntry, assetType AssetType, targets []harness.ID) (Scope, *Violation) {
216		return resolveScope(entry, assetType, targets, harness.HasPerUserLocation)

219	// resolveScope is [ResolveScope] with the roster query as a parameter.
220	//
221	// The seam exists because the roster is data this package cannot vary: today
222	// every recognized harness has a per-user location, so the rule that `user`
223	// scope is refused where one does not exist would have no test at all, and
224	// would be free to rot until the first harness that lacks one is added — which
225	// is exactly when a silent fall back to project scope would start installing
226	// assets somewhere nobody asked for.
227	func resolveScope(
228		entry AssetEntry,
229		assetType AssetType,
230		targets []harness.ID,
231		perUserLocation func(harness.ID) (bool, error),
232	) (Scope, *Violation) {
233		if entry.Scope == "" {
234			return ScopeProject, nil
235		}
236	
237		declared := Scope(entry.Scope)
238		if !slices.Contains(scopes, declared) {
239			return "", assetViolation(entry.Index, "scope",
240				fmt.Sprintf("%s declares the scope %q, which harnaas does not define", assetSubject(entry.Index), entry.Scope),
241				fmt.Sprintf(
242					"Set %q on the entry in %s to one of %s, or remove it to install at %q scope.",
243					"scope", FileName, scopeList(), ScopeProject,
244				),
245			)
246		}
247		if declared == ScopeProject {
248			return ScopeProject, nil
249		}
250	
251		// An instruction is guidance concatenated into a committed memory file, and
252		// what distinguishes it from a rule is surviving a fresh clone inside that
253		// file. At user scope there is no clone and no committed file, so the type
254		// would mean nothing — this is definitional, not a limitation of the
255		// installer.
256		if assetType == AssetTypeInstruction {
257			return "", assetViolation(entry.Index, "scope",
258				fmt.Sprintf(
259					"%s is an %s at %q scope, and an %s exists only inside the project's committed memory file",
260					assetSubject(entry.Index), AssetTypeInstruction, ScopeUser, AssetTypeInstruction,
261				),
262				fmt.Sprintf(
263					"Remove %q from the entry in %s, or declare its %q as %q, which is the type for always-on guidance outside a committed file.",
264					"scope", FileName, "type", AssetTypeRule,
265				),
266			)
267		}
268	
269		var unsupported []string
270		for _, target := range targets {
271			hasLocation, err := perUserLocation(target)
272			if err != nil {
273				// The target is not in the roster, which [ResolveTargets] or
274				// [CheckHarnesses] has already reported against the field that
275				// declared it. Reporting it a second time as a scope problem would
276				// name an edit that does not fix it.
277				continue
278			}
279			if !hasLocation {
280				unsupported = append(unsupported, quoted(string(target)))
281			}
282		}
283	
284		if len(unsupported) > 0 {
285			return "", assetViolation(entry.Index, "scope",
286				fmt.Sprintf(
287					"%s declares %q scope, and %s no unambiguous per-user location",
288					assetSubject(entry.Index), ScopeUser, hasNo(unsupported),
289				),
290				fmt.Sprintf(
291					"Remove %q from the entry in %s so it installs at %q scope, or narrow the entry's %q to harnesses with a per-user location.",
292					"scope", FileName, ScopeProject, "targets",
293				),
294			)
295		}
296	
297		return ScopeUser, nil
298	}

96	// ParseAssetRef parses one asset entry's source string.
97	//
98	// The two accepted forms are distinguished by their prefix rather than by
99	// trying one and falling back to the other, so a string in neither form is
100	// reported as what it is instead of as a failed parse of a form its author
101	// never used.
102	func ParseAssetRef(index int, source string) (AssetRef, *Violation) {

104		case source == "":
105			return AssetRef{}, assetSourceViolation(index,
106				assetSubject(index)+" declares no source",
107				fmt.Sprintf("Give the entry a source in %s. %s", FileName, assetSourceForms),

114			// into the repository, not to add a prefix to the same path.
115			return AssetRef{}, assetSourceViolation(index,
116				fmt.Sprintf("%s names the absolute path %q, and every asset source is relative", assetSubject(index), source),

Extraction takes the subtree the manifest named and produces exactly the path-to-content mapping
